title.narrative: Protecting human security by tackling the vicious cycle of corruption, instability and conflict

description.narrative: Transparency International’s Defence and Security (TI-DS) aims to ensure that defence and security institutions are accountable to their publics and subject to civilian democratic control and oversight and that corruption risks are reduced. Over the 3 years of this programme, using our key tools of capacity development, research, engagement and advocacy, we will work with TI Chapters across North and West Africa (Sahel) region, and with strategic regional and global actors to identify gaps in systems, strengthen the evidence base for what works, offer solutions and policy recommendations, and advocate for the uptake of these, in order to advance the anticorruption and integrity agenda in defence and security frameworks globally, and contribute to the advancement of human security in the region of focus. The programme will focus on three main areas: - A focus on human security – specifically on the integration of anticorruption norms and practices into peacebuilding, development, and human rights.- Strengthening civic engagement on defence and security issues, so that civil society is better equipped to engage with governments and build effective, systemic oversight of defence sectors- gender sensitivity, will allow us to develop the evidence base to define the relationship between (defence sector) corruption, conflict and gender

title.narrative: Evaluation Report of the TI-DS Project: Protecting human security by tackling the vicious cycle of corruption, instability, and conflict.

description.narrative: An Independent Evaluation is commissioned by TI-DS to an independent team of evaluators: Peter Allan, Samuel Afolabi and Liam O’Shea to provide TI-DS, their key donor, and other stakeholders with an assessment and insight into the Project performance. This is done to identify where positive outcomes and impact have been achieved, and where adjustments to the Project may have to be made to improve outcome and impact.ScopeThe scope of the evaluation includes activities implemented under the current iteration of the Project (October 2021 to September 30, 2024) in Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Tunisia and the UN/EU. This includes research and advocacy work undertaken. Lessons from the previous iteration as well as other evaluations and reviews have also been considered.OutputAn evaluation report that examines the outcomes and impact of the Dutch Project whilst assessing how the effectiveness, efficiency, relevance and sustainability of the Project contribute to outcomes and impact. These will be presented within discrete but linked sections within the report leading to findings, conclusions, and recommendations. Key Findings RELEVANCEThere is almost universal agreement that the focus of the TI-DS Project is relevant at all levels i.e. national, regional, and international - it is filling a need. TI is seen as the most appropriate movement – and the TI-DS Project the most appropriate vehicle – to take forward the mandate of highlighting and, in partnership with key actors and stakeholders, tackle corruption in the Defence and Security sector. Whilst its advocacy and general research work is well received, the most relevant jewel in the crown of the Project’s activities is the Government Defence Integrity (GDI) Index. The Project does well in reviewing the GDI methodology, looking to improve its impact through, for example, developing new indicators on gender. All four country case studies (Mali, Niger, Nigeria, and Tunisia) identified that the Project’s goals were relevant to those countries. There are many challenges for national TI Chapter CSOs to work directly with and influence relevant DS sector actors to ensure their Chapter work contributes to the Project’s desired impact that, “Defence and security institutions globally are increasingly accountable to their public and less at risk of corruption”. The Chapter CSOs, through an in-depth and intricate knowledge of their country and DS sector environment manage to keep their activities broadly relevant to the Project’s goal. COHERENCEThe Project has identified where it believes its key priorities lie vis-à-vis developing international relationships to further the prioritisation of anti-corruption measures in the global SSR and DS architecture. Its relationships with the United Nations are strong and it continues to work with the EU through SSR mapping and with NATO primarily – though not exclusively – through the GDI. It has developed relationships with other international and regional bodies including the African Union (AU) and the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). There are still opportunities to examine and potentially exploit within the international community including a more formal partnership with the Geneva Centre for Security Sector Governance (DCAF) noting this requires a willingness to commit from all actors. There are challenges for individual countries and their TI Chapters to cohere on a national level with some in-country actors, often government bodies, unwilling to engage. The extent of this varies from country-to-country. TI Chapters have looked to find solutions where practical and safe to do so. Despite these challenges, the Chapters have been effective in identifying potentially new entry points and creating relationships with appropriate actors that continue to address, sometimes tangentially, corruption in the DS sector. The role of the Project in supporting TI Chapters is positive, giving them advice and assistance when required and the space to create their own approach to tackling corruption.EFFECTIVENESS / IMPACTTwo of the main pillars of the Project’s work when it comes to international engagement are research and advocacy. Neither of these pillars operates in a vacuum and there is a symbiotic relationship between research and advocacy, with each contributing to the other. There is some evidence of progress toward achieving long-term impact by embedding anti-corruption language in appropriate legal instruments, conventions, and guidelines, which is based upon the Project’s influencing strategies. This has helped raise both the awareness, visibility, and prioritisation of the issue. The research work, including the work done on the GDI index which provides a resource for those actors working in SSR and the Defence and Security sector, is universally well-received and has contributed to many project partners’ work in anti-corruption (and broader) SSR work . Challenges remain in the advocacy work regarding arguing for the need to establish the centrality of corruption as it impacts the DS sector with some non-TI stakeholders, questioning the added-value and impact of pursuing this objective over other Project outputs. At the country level, despite difficult operating conditions, the TI Chapters have broadly managed to achieve some effect and impact in specific regions of the country (sometimes nationally), and in various thematic areas. These areas are sometimes tenuously linked to tackling corruption in the DS sector although it has contributed to a general improvement in CSO cooperation and coordination. The Chapters know what relationships can and cannot be pursued and developed, and they have proved nimble in adapting to the constantly changing geo-political landscape. The TI-DS Project ethos of allowing the Chapter to determine its best course of action is well founded and the improving of TI-DS / TI Chapter reporting regime helps ensure Chapter activities provide a clear pathway to tackling corruption in the DS sector. EFFICIENCYThe Project uses the resources that it has in a generally efficient manner. There have been no obvious inefficiencies noted from the financial information provided regarding the allocation of the budget to specific activities. The underspend in the year 2023 was due to the TI-DS strategic refresh which “paused” some activity delivery. The introduction of a Monitoring, Evaluation, and Learning (MEL) Manager for 11 months helped provide the impetus for consolidating and improving learning systems and although these have been maintained they are not fully developed or exploited. However, the regular turnover of staff at TI-DS, crucially linked with a reduction in Project staff numbers, provides efficiency challenges that are not easily overcome. When a staff member leaves, they often take with them institutional knowledge and personal contacts. Whilst both an induction process and handover policy exist their effectiveness could be improved. Additionally, knowledge management within the Project is fragmented with key electronic files kept in different locations. The Project has acknowledged these issues and is taking steps to rectify the situation. The TI Chapters have used the financial contribution of the Project efficiently and there are no concerns from a Project or donor perspective. SUSTAINABILITYConsidering the international research and advocacy work done, all stakeholders saw some sustainability insofar as published research papers remain in the public domain, and advocacy work can embed anti-corruption language into various international, regional, and national legal instruments, conventions, guidelines, etc. Yet some research can become dated and needs to be refreshed. This was most notably highlighted with the work done in determining the GDI index, and whilst baseline GDI research retains some value, and much of the research remains relatively unchanged over the 5-year period, it was perceived that the bulk requires regular renewal. From the country case studies a common sustainability outcome was the recognition that TI Chapter engagement provided those CSO actors with new knowledge and expertise in the sector. This helps build and maintain some pressure on the appropriate government institutions to develop integrity changes and reforms. It also builds a cadre of national advocates who continue to pursue the goals of the Project as an integral part of their professional work. The greatest existential threat to Project sustainability is the lack of a diverse number of donors. Conclusions There is clarity across all TI-DS Project stakeholders, partners, and critical actors within the global, regional, and national anti-corruption community that the Project was – and remains – fully relevant. It is also recognised that TI is the most relevant organisation to take this work forward, given its profile and positive reputation in the anti-corruption environment.In general, the Project coheres well at the international, regional, and national levels. It has mapped those organisations (and individuals within those organisations) whose mandate(s) could potentially add value to the Project’s work. At the national TI Chapter level there are challenges in cohering work between the various national agencies and Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) although the Chapter CSOs do well in mitigating these challenges.The Project has achieved evidenced effectiveness and progress toward its overall impact goal. The Project ethos is built around providing research products and advocating for an anti-corruption focus in the DS sector. The quality of those research products is exceptionally high, and their effectiveness in promoting the overall goal of the Project and assisting partners to achieve their own, related goals is consistently praised. The advocacy work done by the Project in raising the level of awareness and priority given to tackling corruption in the DS sector has moved organisations, most notably the UN, to more engagement with the Project and the topic itself. The Project continues to receive invitations to participate in meetings, roundtables, and consultations with key actors. Yet the value of this type of advocacy work is not universally recognised by some key non-TI stakeholders.The Project has used its financial resources efficiently. The allocation and spending of budget over the life of the Project has been within anticipated parameters. From a national perspective the TI Chapters are viewed as using the Project’s funds in an efficient manner. There is no disquiet from the main donors nor internally from TI-DS Project staff, that funds are being inefficiently or inappropriately used. The Project does suffer from some inefficiencies primarily linked to high staff turnover and shrinking personnel resources which have had an impact on the timelines for the outputs of the various sub-teams. A critical area that was highlighted as fully sustainable was the knowledge that was imparted to Project partners, most notably TI Chapters, who would then take that knowledge into their work regardless of any future Project support. Many of its products are seen as mostly sustainable. The published research products continue to have value long after their publication date although that value will reduce over time if not updated. This message came through most clearly when considering the GDI index. The key existential risk to Project sustainability and the subsequent development and delivery of its activities is the lack of diverse sources of Project funding.The Project can be viewed as successful. It operates in an environment where it is the partner of choice in a subject matter area that is increasingly acknowledged – partly due to the Project itself – as important for improving the safety and security of all global citizens.
